A.explanation: The current is not reduced below normal because the 250 V supply exactly matches the sum $240 \text{ V} + 10 \text{ V}$ for the common normal current.

B.explanation: Both lamps require $0.25 \text{ A}$ at normal brightness, so the series current of $0.25 \text{ A}$ gives each lamp its rated voltage and power.

C.explanation: The 10 V lamp still passes the same series current and develops $10 \text{ V}$ across it, so it also lights normally.

D.explanation: The 10 V lamp does not experience over-voltage because it drops only about $10 \text{ V}$, not the full $250 \text{ V}$.

hints: Calculate the normal operating current of each lamp from its rating using $I = P/V$ with $60 \text{ W}$ at $240 \text{ V}$ and $2.5 \text{ W}$ at $10 \text{ V}$.
Recall that in series the current is the same through both lamps while the supply $250 \text{ V}$ is shared as $V_1 + V_2$.
Check whether the two normal currents match and whether $240 \text{ V} + 10 \text{ V}$ equals the $250 \text{ V}$ supply to decide on brightness or blowing.
walkthrough: Find the current for normal brightness from $I = P/V$ for each lamp.
For the 240 V lamp: $I_1 = 60/240 = 0.25 \text{ A}$. For the 10 V lamp: $I_2 = 2.5/10 = 0.25 \text{ A}$.
Note both lamps are designed to work normally at the same current of $0.25 \text{ A}$, and in series they must carry the same current.
Check voltages: at $0.25 \text{ A}$ the lamps need $240 \text{ V}$ and $10 \text{ V}$, whose sum is $240 + 10 = 250 \text{ V}$, exactly the supply voltage.
Therefore the series circuit can run at $0.25 \text{ A}$ with each lamp at its rated $V$ and $P$, so both light normally. This is option B.
